claim: Pannexin 1 (Panx1) is a membrane channel implicated in numerous physiological and pathophysiological processes via its ability to support release of ATP and other cellular metabolites for local intercellular signaling.
source: Pannexin 1 (Panx1) is a membrane channel implicated in numerous physiological and pathophysiological processes via its ability to support release of ATP and other cellular metabolites for local intercellular signaling.
evidence: This is a general statement about Panx1's role supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: To date, there has been no direct demonstration of large molecule permeation via the Panx1 channel itself.
source: However, to date, there has been no direct demonstration of large molecule permeation via the Panx1 channel itself, and thus the permselectivity of Panx1 for different molecules remains unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in the literature that the current study addresses.

claim: Channel activation by caspase cleavage yields a dye-permeable pore that favors flux of anionic, large-molecule permeants (up to ~1 kDa).
source: To address this, we expressed, purified, and reconstituted Panx1 into proteoliposomes and demonstrated that channel activation by caspase cleavage yields a dye-permeable pore that favors flux of anionic, large-molecule permeants (up to ~1 kDa).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from proteoliposome reconstitution and dye permeation assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: Large cationic molecules can permeate the Panx1 channel, albeit at a much lower rate than anionic molecules.
source: Large cationic molecules can also permeate the channel, albeit at a much lower rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing permeation rates of cationic and anionic dyes.

claim: Panx1 channels provide a molecular pathway for flux of ATP and other anionic (glutamate) and cationic signaling metabolites (spermidine).
source: We further show that Panx1 channels provide a molecular pathway for flux of ATP and other anionic (glutamate) and cationic signaling metabolites (spermidine).
evidence: This is supported by radiolabeled metabolite uptake assays shown in Figure 4.

claim: Panx1 plays a critical role in cell clearance after apoptosis.
source: Among others, this includes cell clearance after apoptosis (Chekeni et al., 2010; Medina et al., 2020; Poon et al., 2014), blood pressure regulation (Billaud et al., 2011; Good et al., 2018a), stroke (Bargiotas et al., 2011; Good et al., 2018b; Thompson, 2015), and neuropathic pain (Bravo et al., 2014; Weaver et al., 2017; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Individual Panx1 subunits consist of a four-transmembrane α-helical bundle with a cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3.
source: Individual Panx1 subunits consist of a four-transmembrane α-helical bundle with a cytoplasmic loop between TM2 and TM3; the N- and C-termini also reside on the cytoplasmic surface (Baranova et al., 2004; Penuela et al., 2013).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to previous structural studies.

claim: Panx1 channels are broadly similar to a subset of mammalian large-pore ion channels that include connexin gap junctions, CALHM1, and SWELL1 (LRRC8).
source: These channels are broadly similar to a subset of mammalian large-pore ion channels that include connexin gap junctions (Panchin et al., 2000), calcium homeostasis modulator 1 (CALHM1) (Siebert et al., 2013; Syrjanen et al., 2020), and SWELL1 (LRRC8) (Abascal and Zardoya, 2012; Deneka et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is supported by citations to studies on related channel families.

claim: Recent cryoEM structures revealed that these different channels exist in a variety of oligomeric states (from hexameric to undecameric).
source: Despite a conserved subunit topology, recent cryoEM structures revealed that these different channels exist in a variety of oligomeric states (from hexameric to undecameric) (Deng et al., 2020; Michalski et al., 2020).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to recent cryoEM studies.

claim: Basal Panx1 activity does not appear to be associated with large molecule permeation.
source: Panx1 ionic currents have occasionally been detected under unstimulated conditions (Ma et al., 2012; Romanov et al., 2012; Ruan et al., 2020), but that basal activity does not appear to be associated with large molecule permeation (Romanov et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: Caspase-mediated cleavage of Panx1 C-tails during apoptosis or pyroptosis is accompanied by uptake of dyes indicative of cell death and release of ATP and UTP that serve as 'find-me' signals.
source: Among these, caspase-mediated activation is a well-characterized mechanism in which cleavage of the channel C-tails, as occurs during apoptosis or pyroptosis, is accompanied by uptake of dyes indicative of cell death (e.g., Yo-Pro-1 and To-Pro-3) and release of ATP and UTP that serve as 'find-me' signals to direct phagocytic clearance of cell corpses (Chekeni et al., 2010; Chiu et al., 2017; Poon et al., 2014; Qu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies on caspase-mediated activation and cell death signaling.

claim: Panx1 cleavage elicits efflux of additional metabolites from apoptotic cells, which function as local 'good-bye' signals with anti-inflammatory, wound healing, and cell proliferative actions.
source: Moreover, Panx1 cleavage elicits efflux of additional metabolites from apoptotic cells, which function as local 'good-bye' signals with anti-inflammatory, wound healing, and cell proliferative actions (Medina et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a study on metabolite release from apoptotic cells.

claim: All previous studies on Panx1 large molecule permeation have been performed using intact cells, not demonstrating that permeation occurs directly via the channel itself.
source: Notably, all studies to date have been performed using intact cells. Therefore, this previous work does not demonstrate that large molecule permeation occurs directly via the channel itself or exclude a secondary release mechanism.
evidence: This identifies a limitation in previous research that the current study addresses.

claim: Recently available Panx1 channel structures from both intact and caspase-cleaved channels reveal a central pore with an extracellular constriction that has a diameter of ~9 Å.
source: Moreover, recently available Panx1 channel structures from both intact (inactive) and caspase-cleaved (activated) channels reveal a central pore with an extracellular constriction that has a diameter of ~9 Å, which would appear to be too small to enable large molecule permeation (Deng et al., 2020; Jin et al., 2020; Michalski et al., 2020; Mou et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citations to multiple recent cryoEM studies.

claim: The frog Panx1 (fPanx1) ortholog from Xenopus tropicalis was used in this study.
source: For these studies, we used the Panx1 ortholog from Xenopus tropicalis (i.e., frog Panx1 and fPanx1) that has been examined in recent structural studies (Deng et al., 2020; Michalski et al., 2020).
evidence: This describes the experimental system used, supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: Purified fPanx1-eGFP was successfully incorporated into proteoliposomes.
source: Purified fPanx1-eGFP was incorporated into proteoliposomes that appeared in fractions 1–3 of a co-floatation assay on a Nycodenz density gradient (Figure 1B,C; Hernandez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B,C demonstrating successful reconstitution.

claim: Proteoliposomes had a mean diameter of 97.3 ± 22 nm.
source: When analyzed by negative-stain electron microscopy, we observed a normal distribution of circular proteoliposomes in projection images, with the expected mean diameter of 97.3 ± 22 nm (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy measurements shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Purified fPanx1 incorporated into proteoliposomes was cleaved at the expected sites following overnight incubation with recombinant Caspase-3.
source: Therefore, we verified that purified fPanx1 incorporated into proteoliposomes was cleaved at the expected sites following overnight incubation with recombinant Caspase-3 (Casp3) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Cleavage at the C-terminal site is necessary and sufficient for Panx1 channel activation.
source: Note that although the channel can be cleaved at multiple sites, cleavage at the C-terminal site is necessary and sufficient for channel activation (Chekeni et al., 2010; Chiu et al., 2017; Sandilos et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on caspase cleavage sites.

claim: fPanx1 was basally silent in HEK293T cells and could be activated by intracellular dialysis with Casp3 to generate whole cell currents with an outwardly-rectifying current–voltage profile.
source: In recordings from transfected HEK293T cells, we found that fPanx1 was basally silent and could be activated by intracellular dialysis with Casp3 to generate whole cell currents with an outwardly-rectifying current–voltage profile (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B) similar to that observed with cleavage-activated human Panx1 (hPANX1) channels (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C; Chiu et al., 2017; Sandilos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Caspase-activated fPanx1 currents were blocked by the Panx1 inhibitor carbenoxolone (CBX).
source: These currents were blocked by the Panx1 inhibitor carbenoxolone (CBX).
evidence: This is supported by electrophysiological data showing CBX inhibition.

claim: Single fPanx1 channels were silent in excised inside-out patches until activated by Casp3 and displayed a unitary conductance of 91.4 ± 13.5 pS.
source: In addition, and also similar to hPANX1, single fPanx1 channels were silent in excised inside-out patches until activated by Casp3 (Chiu et al., 2017); the cleavage-activated channels were inhibited by CBX and displayed a unitary conductance of 91.4 ± 13.5 pS (N = 3, Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This is supported by single-channel electrophysiological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: Whole cell and single channel properties of fPanx1 are essentially identical to hPANX1 after caspase activation.
source: Thus, whole cell and single channel properties of fPanx1 are essentially identical to hPANX1 after caspase activation (Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of electrophysiological data between fPanx1 and hPANX1.

claim: Prior to application of caspase, large 'flickery' currents were occasionally observed at extreme potentials in lipid bilayers containing fPanx1.
source: Prior to application of caspase, large 'flickery' currents were occasionally observed at extreme potentials (e.g., +140 mV; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A), and this often signified successful incorporation of fPanx1 into the bilayer.
evidence: This is supported by bilayer recording data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Before caspase addition, fPanx1 channel activity was not observed at physiological potentials in lipid bilayers.
source: However, before caspase addition, fPanx1 channel activity was not observed at physiological potentials, even in a bath solution containing 200 mM K+ (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by bilayer recording data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: After caspase addition, channel currents with discrete openings and closings became apparent across a wide range of physiological voltages in lipid bilayers.
source: After caspase addition, channel currents with discrete openings and closings became apparent across a wide range of physiological voltages (Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B)
evidence: This is supported by bilayer recording data shown in Figure 1F and Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Caspase-activated fPanx1 channels in bilayers displayed two distinct conductance levels: ~100 pS and ~189 pS.
source: The individual bilayers usually included multiple active channels that presented with either of two distinct conductance levels: one set had a unitary conductance of ~100 pS, similar to that recorded in mammalian cells, and the second displayed a larger unitary conductance of ~189 pS (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by conductance measurements from bilayer recordings shown in Figure 1G.

claim: The open channel I-V relationships for caspase-activated fPanx1 in bilayers were approximately ohmic.
source: For both, the open channel I-V relationships were approximately ohmic (Figure 1G), unlike the outwardly-rectifying single channel conductance observed for recombinant caspase-activated Panx1 in mammalian cells (Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by I-V relationship data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Uptake of SR-B into liposomes was observed only when they contained fPanx1 and were treated with caspase.
source: Uptake of SR-B into liposomes was observed only when they contained fPanx1 and were treated with caspase.
evidence: This is supported by dye uptake assay data.

claim: Dye uptake was inhibited when caspase-treated fPanx1-containing proteoliposomes were treated with CBX.
source: In addition, dye uptake was inhibited when caspase-treated fPanx1-containing proteoliposomes were treated with CBX before and during the dye incubation period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by dye uptake assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: SR-B was only observed in proteoliposomes that were treated with Casp3 as shown by ImageStream flow cytometry.
source: As depicted in the representative images (Figure 2B), SR-B was only observed in proteoliposomes that were treated with Casp3.
evidence: This is supported by ImageStream flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Compared to untreated proteoliposomes, a larger fraction of Casp3-treated proteoliposomes contained SR-B (83.6% vs. 20.4%) at ~10-fold higher MFI levels.
source: Compared to untreated proteoliposomes, a larger fraction of Casp3-treated proteoliposomes contained SR-B (83.6% vs. 20.4%; Figure 2C) and at ~10-fold higher MFI levels.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A modest leftward shift in the GFP signal after caspase treatment reflects cleavage of the outward-facing fPanx1 C-tail and removal of the C-terminal GFP tag.
source: We found a concomitant, albeit modest, leftward shift in the GFP signal after caspase treatment, reflecting cleavage of the outward-facing fPanx1 C-tail (exposed to caspase) and the associated removal of the C-terminal GFP tag (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2C and is an inference from the experimental design.

claim: Caspase-cleaved fPanx1 channels generate a pore that is large enough for permeation of the SR-B dye.
source: In multiple independent experiments and proteoliposome preparations, Casp3 treatment of fPanx1 proteoliposomes resulted in a decrease in GFP signal and a concomitant increase in SR-B signal (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), indicating that caspase-cleaved fPanx1 channels generate a pore that is large enough for permeation of the SR-B dye.
evidence: This is supported by multiple independent experiments shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: RhB was released from proteoliposomes in a manner dependent on caspase-mediated cleavage of fPanx1.
source: Like SR-B, RhB was released from proteoliposomes, and this release was also dependent on caspase-mediated cleavage of fPanx1 (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The rate of dye efflux was positively correlated with the fraction of fPanx1 cleavage for both SR-B and RhB dyes.
source: The rate of dye efflux, obtained from fits to mono-exponential decay curves of the fluorescent signal for each proteoliposome, was positively correlated with the fraction of fPanx1 cleavage (i.e., reduction in GFP fluorescence) for both SR-B and RhB dyes (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Despite the smaller size of RhB, the efflux rate was significantly slower than for SR-B due to the cationic charge.
source: Notably, despite the smaller size of RhB, the efflux rate was significantly slower than for SR-B due to the cationic charge (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of dye efflux rates shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Larger anionic dyes (Alexa 594 and Alexa 555) permeated caspase-cleaved fPanx1 at rates substantially slower than the smaller SR-B.
source: These larger dyes permeated caspase-cleaved fPanx1 at rates substantially slower than the smaller SR-B (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by comparative dye efflux rate data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Despite being approximately two times larger, anionic dyes Alexa 594 and Alexa 555 transited the channel at rates comparable to the cationic dye RhB.
source: Of note, however, despite being approximately two times larger, these anionic dyes transited the channel at rates comparable to the cationic dye RhB (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by comparative dye efflux rate data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: ATTO550 (1363 Da) and Dextran 3000 (3000 Da) were unable to permeate caspase-activated fPanx1.
source: Finally, we also examined two larger dyes (ATTO 550 (+), 1363 Da; and Dextran 3000 (−), 3000 Da; Figure 3—figure supplement 1), and neither of those were able to permeate caspase-activated fPanx1 (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is supported by dye permeation data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: The channel favors anionic over cationic permeants.
source: Together, these data indicate that the channel favors anionic over cationic permeants and reveal that the pore size is sufficient to accommodate molecules up to 980 Da.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparative dye permeation data.

claim: The pore size of caspase-activated fPanx1 is sufficient to accommodate molecules up to 980 Da.
source: Together, these data indicate that the channel favors anionic over cationic permeants and reveal that the pore size is sufficient to accommodate molecules up to 980 Da.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dye permeation data showing Alexa 555 (980 Da) can permeate but ATTO 550 (1363 Da) cannot.

claim: Uptake of α-[32P]ATP, [3H]-glutamate, and [3H]-spermidine into proteoliposomes required caspase-activated fPanx1.
source: Indeed, we found that uptake of α-[32P]ATP, [3H]-glutamate, and [3H]-spermidine into proteoliposomes required caspase-activated fPanx1; uptake was not observed when liposomes did not contain fPanx1 or when the channel was not activated by Casp3 (Figure 4B–D).
evidence: This is supported by radiolabeled metabolite uptake assay data shown in Figure 4B-D.

claim: Both ATP and spermidine can flux via caspase-activated Panx1 when included together in the same assay.
source: We also tested whether ATP and spermidine could flux via caspase-activated Panx1 when included together in the same assay, rather than independently. Under these conditions, we again found uptake of both ATP and spermidine into caspase-cleaved Panx1-containing proteoliposomes, albeit at slightly lower levels (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by concurrent metabolite uptake assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Cleavage-activated fPanx1 itself is sufficient to form a membrane conduit capable of conducting ATP and other important signaling metabolites.
source: These data indicate that cleavage-activated fPanx1 itself is sufficient to form a membrane conduit capable of conducting ATP and other important signaling metabolites.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the metabolite uptake data.

claim: Different conductance levels for channels attributed to Panx1 have been observed in various cell systems after different forms of activation, reportedly up to ~500 pS.
source: However, different conductance levels for channels attributed to Panx1 have been observed in various cell systems after different forms of activation, reportedly up to ~500 pS (Bao et al., 2004; reviewed in Chiu et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous electrophysiological studies.

claim: In lipid bilayer recordings of purified hPANX1, Mou et al. detected a ~30 pS channel in E. coli polar lipid extract in the absence of specific activation.
source: In lipid bilayer recordings of purified hPANX1 reported during preparation of this work, Mou et al. detected a ~ 30 pS channel in E. coli polar lipid extract, although these recordings were in the absence of any specific form of activation and were not accompanied by open-closed transitions; the C-tail-cleaved channels, by contrast, yielded a number of extremely large open channel conductance states (i.e., 750 pS, 1.3 nS, and 1.8 nS; at +100 mV) (Mou et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a concurrent study by Mou et al.

claim: Constitutive Panx1 channel activity displays a unitary conductance similar to that of channels stimulated by Casp3 cleavage (~70–80 pS) but does not appear to support ATP release.
source: There have been other reports of constitutive Panx1 channel activity (i.e., in the absence of stimulation), and although these channels display a unitary conductance similar to that of channels stimulated by Casp3 cleavage (~70–80 pS), they do not appear to support ATP release (Ma et al., 2012; Romanov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies on constitutive Panx1 activity.

claim: A second permeation pathway, visible as a side tunnel in the structure of hPANX1, could support atomic ion flux through unstimulated and C-tail-intact channels in the absence of large molecule permeation.
source: It was recently proposed that a second permeation pathway, visible as a side tunnel in the structure of hPANX1, could support atomic ion flux through unstimulated and C-tail-intact channels in the absence of large molecule permeation (Ruan et al., 2020)
evidence: This is a proposal from a cited study that requires further exploration.

claim: In ion substitution experiments, obvious shifts in reversal potential (Erev) were observed when Cl− was exchanged with other negatively charged counterions.
source: In ion substitution experiments, obvious shifts in reversal potential (Erev) were observed when Cl− was exchanged with other negatively charged counterions (Ma et al., 2012; Michalski et al., 2020; Romanov et al., 2012; Ruan et al., 2020; Wang and Dahl, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous ion substitution studies.

claim: Shifts in Erev were strongly affected by mutations in R75, a positively charged residue next to W74, the narrowest pore constriction site.
source: These shifts in Erev were strongly affected by mutations in R75, a positively charged residue next to W74, the narrowest pore constriction site identified in multiple recent structural reports (Deng et al., 2020; Michalski et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to mutagenesis and structural studies.

claim: Negligible changes in Erev accompany substitution with different positively charged counterions.
source: By contrast, negligible changes in Erev accompany substitution with different positively charged counterions (Michalski et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to ion substitution studies.

claim: It has been inferred that the Panx1 channel is exclusively anion-selective and impermeable to cations.
source: On this basis, it has been inferred that the channel is exclusively anion-selective and impermeable to cations (Ma et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a previous inference from the literature that the current study challenges.

claim: Previous studies have predicted the maximum size of a Panx1 permeant to be less than 1270 Da (7-AAD) or 1500 Da (PEG 1500).
source: Previous studies have predicted the maximum size of a Panx1 permeant to be less than 1270 Da (7-AAD) (Chiu et al., 2017; Poon et al., 2014) or 1500 Da (PEG 1500) (Wang et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous permeability studies.

claim: Alexa555 (980 Da) could transit via the cleavage-activated Panx1 channel while ATTO550 (1363 Da) was unable to permeate.
source: We found that Alexa555 (980 Da) could transit via the cleavage-activated Panx1 channel while ATTO550 (1363 Da) was unable to permeate.
evidence: This is supported by dye permeation data from TIRF microscopy experiments.

claim: The pore of the activated Panx1 channel must be able to accommodate a molecule at least up to ~1 kDa.
source: This confirms that the pore of the activated channel must be able to accommodate a molecule at least up to ~1 kDa.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the dye permeation data.

claim: The architecture and contours of the transmembrane pore were remarkably similar for all Panx1 constructs analyzed in recent cryoEM structures, despite including full length and C-terminal cleaved/truncated forms.
source: The architecture and contours of the transmembrane pore were remarkably similar for all constructs analyzed, despite those including full length (presumably inactive) and C-terminal cleaved/truncated (presumably activated) (Deng et al., 2020; Michalski et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple cryoEM structural studies.

claim: The narrowest pore constriction was formed by a ring of seven W74 residues on the extracellular surface of the channel, with a diameter of ~8–10 Å.
source: The narrowest pore constriction was formed by a ring of seven W74 residues on the extracellular surface of the channel, with a diameter of ~8–10 Å.
evidence: This structural information is based on cryoEM structures cited in the manuscript.

claim: The narrowest constriction appears to be too small to accommodate large dyes or even hydrated ATP, although this may be influenced by the shape and flexibility of the permeant molecule and/or the pore itself.
source: This constriction appears to be too small to accommodate large dyes or even hydrated ATP, although this may be influenced by the shape and flexibility of the permeant molecule and/or the pore itself.
evidence: This is a speculation based on structural data and the observed permeation properties.

claim: Upon activation by cleavage at the C-terminal caspase site, Panx1 transitions between open and closed states.
source: Moreover, upon activation by cleavage (or truncation) at the C-terminal caspase site, Panx1 transitions between open and closed states (Chiu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous electrophysiological study.

claim: The available Panx1 structures may have captured the channel in a state that is 'open' for atomic ions but remains 'closed' for large molecules.
source: Thus, the available structures may have captured the channel in a state that is 'open' for atomic ions but remains 'closed' for large molecules.
evidence: This is a speculation to reconcile structural and functional data.

claim: The possibility of multiple open conformations or separate permeation pathways for ions and large molecules in both Panx1 channels and in CALHM1 channels have been proposed.
source: The possibility of multiple open conformations or separate permeation pathways for ions and large molecules in both Panx1 channels and in CALHM1 channels have been proposed (Gaete et al., 2020; Nielsen et al., 2020; Ruan et al., 2020; Wang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies proposing multiple conformational states.

claim: Panx1 cleavage by caspase is permissive for conformations that allow large molecule permeation, perhaps by removing a physical block to pore access while allowing open-closed transitions.
source: If those distinct conformations exist, the dye/metabolite flux we present indicates that Panx1 cleavage by caspase is permissive for conformations that allow large molecule permeation, perhaps by removing a physical block to pore access while allowing open-closed transitions (Sandilos et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a mechanistic speculation based on the experimental data and cited structural considerations.

claim: Molecules up to ~1 kDa are capable of permeating caspase cleavage-activated fPanx1.
source: Examination of dye and metabolite flux through purified Panx1 channels reconstituted in proteoliposomes demonstrates directly that molecules up to ~1 kDa are capable of permeating caspase cleavage-activated fPanx1.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the dye and metabolite permeation data.

claim: Anionic and cationic metabolites and dyes can traverse caspase-activated Panx1 channels, albeit with a marked preference for anionic molecules.
source: Moreover, anionic and cationic metabolites and dyes can traverse caspase-activated Panx1 channels, albeit with a marked preference for anionic molecules.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the comparative permeation data for charged molecules.

claim: These data validate caspase-activated Panx1 as a direct conduit for release of ATP and other signaling molecules that facilitate immunologically silent cell clearance in the context of caspase-dependent cell death.
source: These data validate caspase-activated Panx1 as a direct conduit for release of ATP and other signaling molecules that facilitate immunologically silent cell clearance in the context of caspase-dependent cell death (apoptosis, pyroptosis) (Chekeni et al., 2010; Medina et al., 2020; Qu et al., 2011; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a summary conclusion that integrates the current findings with previous studies on Panx1's physiological roles.
